title: The Passover and the Night Israel Went Free
summary: God gives Moses and Aaron instructions for the first Passover: each household is to kill an unblemished lamb, put its blood on the doorframe, and eat the meat roasted with unleavened bread and bitter herbs, dressed and ready to leave. At midnight the LORD strikes down the firstborn of Egypt and passes over the houses marked with blood. Pharaoh sends Israel out that night, the Egyptians give them silver, gold, and clothing, and after 430 years in Egypt the Israelites march out from Rameses, with rules added for how the Passover is to be kept forever.
story: Everything in Exodus so far has been leading to this night. God warned Pharaoh in 4:23 that he would kill his firstborn if he did not let God's firstborn go, and the nine plagues were warnings that Pharaoh refused. Now the tenth plague falls, and it falls differently from the others. Israel is not automatically exempt. Protection comes through a lamb, its blood, and a meal eaten in obedience. The chapter moves back and forth between that first night and every later Passover, because the event and its remembrance belong together. By the end Israel is out of Egypt, a vast company on the road from Rameses to Succoth, and the book's first great movement, from slavery to release, is complete. The sea still lies ahead (chapter 14), and Sinai beyond it.
historical:
The Passover falls in spring, in the month called Abib (13:4; Deuteronomy 16:1), a word connected with fresh ears of grain. After the Babylonian exile the Jews adopted Babylonian month names, and the same month is called Nisan (Nehemiah 2:1). Verse 2 makes it the first month of the year: Israel's calendar of worship would begin with its redemption. Since Israel's months began with the new moon, the fourteenth day fell at the full moon, so the night of the Passover was a moonlit one. The lamb was to be killed at twilight, literally between the two evenings; by the time of the Second Temple this was understood as the afternoon, when the lambs were slaughtered at the temple.

Verse 37 has Israel leaving from Rameses, the Delta city of the store cities in 1:11, usually identified with Pi-Ramesses, the capital built by Ramesses II, and going to Succoth, often located near the Wadi Tumilat on the route east. The number of about 600,000 men on foot, besides women and children, would mean a total population of two million or more. Some interpreters take the figure as it stands; others argue that the Hebrew word for thousand can also mean a clan or military unit, which would make the company much smaller (see the introduction to Exodus). The 430 years of verse 40 are also counted in more than one way. The Hebrew text says the Israelites lived in Egypt 430 years; the ancient Greek translation and the Samaritan Pentateuch include the patriarchs' time in Canaan in the same span, and Paul's reckoning of 430 years from the promise to the law (Galatians 3:17) fits that longer count. Genesis 15:13 gives the round figure of four hundred years.
cultural:
The Passover is a family meal. Each household takes a lamb or kid, a year-old male without blemish from the sheep or the goats, and neighbors share if the family is small (verses 3 to 5). The animal was the best of the flock, not a leftover. It was roasted whole, not boiled, and eaten entirely that night. The bread was unleavened, made without the piece of fermented dough from a previous batch that ordinarily made bread rise, and the herbs were bitter. Later Jewish tradition read the bitter herbs as a taste of the bitterness of slavery, since 1:14 says the Egyptians made Israel's lives bitter using the same Hebrew root. Deuteronomy calls the unleavened loaves “the bread of affliction” (Deuteronomy 16:3), eaten in haste. The instruction to remove all leaven from the house (verse 15) is the origin of the Jewish custom of searching the house for leaven before Passover.

The blood was applied with hyssop, a small bushy plant (probably a kind of marjoram) used elsewhere for sprinkling in rites of cleansing; a psalmist prays, “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean” (Psalm 51:7). It went on the doorposts and the lintel, the frame through which anyone entering the house had to pass. The Hebrew word for doorpost, mezuzah, later gave its name to the small case holding verses of Scripture that Jewish families fix to their doorframes (see Deuteronomy 6:9). Finally, the rules in verses 43 to 49 show that Israel was open to outsiders from the start. A foreigner who wished to keep the Passover could do so once the males of his household were circumcised, and then “he shall be like a native of the land.”
literary: The chapter weaves narrative and instruction together. The actual events of the night take only eight verses (verses 29 to 36), while instructions surround them: for the first Passover (verses 1 to 13), for the Feast of Unleavened Bread in later years (verses 14 to 20), for the elders (verses 21 to 28), and for who may eat (verses 43 to 49). The weaving is deliberate. The event is told so that it can be kept, and the phrase “for the generations to come” recurs (verses 14, 17, and 42). Verse 26 imagines a child asking, “What does this service mean to you?” It is one of several such questions in Exodus 13 and Deuteronomy 6:20, and the Passover Haggadah, the order of service for the Jewish Passover meal, builds its teaching of the children on them. Other details carry weight. Pharaoh, regarded as a god, ends his last speech by asking Moses, “And bless me also” (verse 32). Israel marches out as “the LORD’s divisions” (verse 41), an army leaving at the end of the 430 years “to the very day.” And because the LORD “kept a vigil” that night, Israel keeps it as a vigil too (verse 42), the Hebrew using the same word for God's watch and theirs.

outline.t: The first Passover: the lamb and the blood
The Feast of Unleavened Bread for all generations
Moses instructs the elders, and the people worship
The death of the firstborn and Israel's release
From Rameses to Succoth after 430 years

doctrines.note: Israel's firstborn are protected by the blood of a lamb that dies in their place, and the rite is called “the Passover sacrifice to the LORD” (verse 27). Israel's safety rests not on its own innocence but on the blood God provided, a pattern the sacrificial laws of Leviticus develop and the New Testament sees fulfilled in Christ.

The Passover is a meal commanded as a memorial for all generations (verse 14), in which each generation takes part in the original rescue. Jesus instituted the Lord's Supper at a Passover meal. Christians differ over how Christ is present in the Supper, but they agree that it proclaims his death as the fulfillment of what the Passover anticipated.

God says, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (verse 13). Salvation is God's act, received by trusting his word and obeying it: kill the lamb, mark the door, stay inside. And the same law applies to the native and the foreigner (verse 49), so God's saving community is open to all who come under the covenant sign.

“I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt” (verse 12). The last plague is not only on Egypt's people but on the powers Egypt trusted, including the divine king whose own heir dies. Judgment and rescue happen on the same night by the same hand.

words.note: Pasach, to pass over, the verb behind the noun pesach, Passover. Most translations take it as the LORD passing by or skipping the marked houses. Some scholars point to Isaiah 31:5, where the LORD will protect Jerusalem “Like birds hovering overhead” and will pass over it and preserve it, and argue that the verb can also mean to stand guard over. Both senses fit verse 23, where the LORD passes over the door and does not allow the destroyer to enter.

Matstsah, unleavened bread, flat bread baked without leaven. It was the bread of haste, since the people left before their dough could rise (verses 34 and 39). Because a small piece of leaven works through a whole batch of dough, leaven later became a picture of the way corruption spreads, and Paul urges the church to keep the feast “with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth” (1 Corinthians 5:8).

Zikkaron, a memorial or reminder. The Passover day is to be “a memorial for you” (verse 14). In the Bible remembering is not merely recalling a fact but acting on it and taking part in it, so that each generation keeping the Passover says, in effect, this is what the LORD did for me (13:8).

Erev, a mixture, in the phrase mixed multitude (verse 38). A crowd of non-Israelites left Egypt with Israel. The text does not say who they were; they may have included other foreign laborers and Egyptians who had come to fear the LORD (9:20). Their presence helps explain why the Passover rules immediately address foreigners (verses 43 to 49). A group called the rabble appears among the people again in Numbers 11:4.

christ: The New Testament reads Jesus' death through this chapter more than through any other in Exodus. Paul writes, “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). John reports that the soldiers did not break Jesus' legs and sees in it the rule for the Passover lamb in verse 46: “Not one of His bones will be broken” (John 19:36). Peter speaks of believers redeemed “with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1 Peter 1:19), echoing the unblemished lamb of verse 5. Jesus himself chose a Passover meal to institute the Lord's Supper, speaking of the cup as “the new covenant in My blood” (Luke 22:20). The Gospels describe the timing differently. Matthew, Mark, and Luke present the Last Supper as a Passover meal (Mark 14:12), while John places Jesus' death on “the day of Preparation for the Passover” (John 19:14), when the lambs were being killed. Scholars explain the difference in several ways, including different calendars in use at the time, different meanings of the word Preparation, or John's theological emphasis, but all four Gospels tie Jesus' death to the Passover. What the blood on Israel's doors did on one night in Egypt, the New Testament says Christ's death does for all who belong to him.

hard.q: Why did God require blood on the doorframes, and what did the Passover rite mean?
hard.a:
God hardly needed a mark to know which houses were Israel's. The Hebrew of verse 13 says the blood will be a sign for you, that is, for Israel. Its first purpose was to call for trust. To kill a lamb, mark the door, and stay inside through the night was to take God at his word and act on it, and Hebrews 11:28 calls Moses' keeping of the Passover an act of faith. Its second purpose concerns substitution. Israel's firstborn were not spared because Israelites were better than Egyptians; the judgment passed over houses where a lamb had died. Many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, see here the principle of a life given for a life that the laws of sacrifice develop. Others stress that the Passover is not an atoning sacrifice in the same sense as the sin offering of Leviticus, but a protective, covenant-marking meal whose focus is deliverance and belonging rather than forgiveness. Both emphases have support in the text, which calls the rite a sacrifice (verse 27) and centers it on a family meal.

Historians of religion have also asked where the rite came from. Many critical scholars think Israel's Passover drew on an older springtime rite of shepherds, meant to protect the household and the flock at the season of moving to new pastures, and that Israel's tradition joined it to the exodus and gave it new meaning. Others see no need for such a background and take the chapter as describing the rite's institution. On either view, what Israel celebrated was not a seasonal charm but the night the LORD judged Egypt's gods and brought his people out.

questions: The Passover was meant to be explained to children who ask, “What does this service mean to you?” How would you answer that question about the practices of your own faith?
Israel was protected not because they were better than the Egyptians but because of the lamb's blood. How should that shape the way believers regard people outside the faith?
The same law applied to the native-born and to the foreigner who joined Israel (verse 49). What does that say about who belongs among God's people?
